data.q: Which function creates a new empty Context that is never canceled, has no values, and has no deadline?
data.e: context.Background() returns a nil Context that is typically used as the root of a Context tree in main, init, and tests. context.TODO() is similar but signals that the choice of context is not yet decided.

A new Context and a Done channel
A new Context and an error
data.e: context.WithCancel returns a copy of the parent Context with a new Done channel, and a CancelFunc that, when called, closes the Done channel to signal cancellation.

data.q: How do you properly handle a Context cancellation in a long-running function?
o: Ignore the Context and run to completion
Select on ctx.Done() and return when closed
Call ctx.Err() in a loop without blocking
Use time.Sleep and check ctx.Err() periodically
data.e: The idiomatic pattern is to use a select statement with ctx.Done() to wait for cancellation, then return ctx.Err() which will be context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded.

data.q: Which function creates a Context that automatically cancels after a specified duration?
data.e: context.WithTimeout is a convenience wrapper around WithDeadline that uses time.Now().Add(timeout). It returns a Context and a CancelFunc.

data.q: What is the return type of ctx.Done()?
data.e: ctx.Done() returns a read-only channel (<-chan struct{}) that is closed when the Context is canceled or times out. Receiving from this channel signals that the work should stop.

data.q: After a Context is canceled, what does ctx.Err() return?
o: Either context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded depending on the cause
data.e: ctx.Err() returns nil if the Context is not yet done. If done, it returns context.Canceled if canceled explicitly, or context.DeadlineExceeded if the deadline passed.

data.q: What is the primary purpose of context.WithValue(parent Context, key, val interface{})?
o: To pass request-scoped data like trace IDs or authentication tokens
To set a deadline for the Context
To create a derived Context that cancels when the parent cancels
data.e: context.WithValue is for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries, such as trace IDs, user IDs, or auth tokens. It should not be used for optional function parameters or shared mutable state.

data.q: What is the recommended type for Context keys to avoid collisions?
o: A custom unexported type (e.g., type contextKey string)
data.e: Using a custom unexported type (like type contextKey string) prevents key collisions across packages. The value can still be a string, but the type ensures uniqueness.

data.q: When should you call the CancelFunc returned by context.WithCancel, WithTimeout, or WithDeadline?
o: Never, the garbage collector handles it
Always, to release resources and allow the Context to be garbage collected
Only when the parent Context is canceled
data.e: Always call the CancelFunc when the operation completes (success or failure) to avoid leaking resources like timers or goroutines waiting on the Done channel. Defer cancel() is the common pattern.

data.q: What happens if you call the CancelFunc multiple times?
o: Subsequent calls are no-ops (safe to call multiple times)
data.e: The CancelFunc is idempotent; calling it more than once has no additional effect and does not panic. This makes it safe to call in multiple cleanup paths.

data.q: How do you propagate a Context through an HTTP server handler chain?
o: Store it in a global variable
Pass it as a function argument to each handler
Use r.Context() and r.WithContext(ctx) on the *http.Request
data.e: In net/http, the request carries the Context. Use r.Context() to retrieve it and r.WithContext(newCtx) to create a new request with a derived Context for the next handler.

data.q: Which standard library package uses Context extensively for timeouts and cancellation?
data.e: database/sql uses Context for query timeouts and cancellation (e.g., QueryContext, ExecContext). Many other packages like net/http, net, and os/exec also support Context.

data.q: What is the difference between context.Background() and context.TODO()?
o: Background() is cancelable, TODO() is not
TODO() has a deadline, Background() does not
They are functionally identical; TODO() signals uncertainty about which Context to use
Background() is for tests, TODO() is for production
data.e: Both return a nil Context that is never canceled. TODO() is a semantic marker for code that should eventually pass a proper Context but hasn't been refactored yet. Static analysis tools may flag TODO() usage.

data.q: How do you create a Context that is canceled when either the parent is canceled OR a deadline passes?
o: Both A and B achieve this
data.e: Both WithDeadline and WithTimeout return a Context that is canceled when the parent cancels OR the deadline/timeout expires, whichever happens first. WithTimeout is just a convenience for relative durations.

data.q: What is a common mistake when using context.WithValue?
o: Using a string literal as the key
data.e: context.WithValue should only be used for request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries (e.g., trace IDs, auth tokens). Using it for optional function parameters hides dependencies and makes code harder to test and understand.

data.q: In a select statement with multiple cases including ctx.Done(), what happens if ctx.Done() is ready and another case is also ready?
o: Go pseudo-randomly selects one of the ready cases
data.e: When multiple cases in a select are ready, Go chooses one at random (pseudo-random uniform selection). This ensures fairness. You cannot rely on ctx.Done() being prioritized.
